URUK — a multi-tenant CMS where a website is data, not code edit this page over MCP · no deploy required

Uruk — a multi-tenant CMS

A website is
data, not code.

Uruk composes entire sites from rows in Postgres — element trees rendered to HTML, cached until the data changes, edited by people and AI agents over the same API. No templates to commit. No build to run. No deploy to wait for.

sh — get running
$ git clone https://github.com/Galaktis/uruk && cd uruk
$ docker compose up
# http://localhost:8000 → this site, served from rows

Why the first city of writing lends its name

From tablet to page

Three moves, same as 3200 BC

A scribe pressed records into clay; a renderer presses rows into HTML. The pipeline is short enough to hold in your head.

01 · WRITE

Rows, not files

Every block on this page is an Element row — a kind, JSON parameters, content, and a parent. Pages are rows too, arranged in a URL tree.

{
  "kind": "heading",
  "content": "A website is data",
  "parameters": { "level": 1 },
  "parent_id": "0198…root"
}
02 · RENDER

The tree becomes HTML

A small library of committed renderers walks the element tree. Text is escaped by default; there are no per-site templates anywhere.

# the only committed "template"
@register("heading")
def heading(el, children, ctx):
    return format_html(
        "<h{0}>{1}</h{0}>",
        el.parameters["level"], el.content)
03 · CACHE

Cached until a row changes

Each render records which elements it touched. Saving one element evicts exactly the pages that used it — a shared header invalidates everywhere at once.

element.save()
└─ PageDependency reverse index
   └─ evict: /  /manifesto  …
✓ next request re-renders once

What the city provides

One deployment, many sites

A single Uruk serves any number of tenants. Each one is a walled district: its own schema, its own users, its own everything.

A schema per tenant

The Host header picks the tenant; the connection's search_path does the isolation. Users, content, and tokens never share tables across sites.

Exact invalidation

The hard problem, solved with a dependency graph: every render records what it read, so one edit evicts precisely the affected pages — nothing more, nothing stale.

Agents are editors

The first admin client is an MCP server, not a dashboard. An agent authenticates as a tenant user and can do exactly what that user's permissions allow.

Sites that travel

Every row has a UUIDv7 key, so a whole site exports as one JSON archive and restores anywhere without collisions. This very site ships as one.

Assets live in the DB

The CSS styling this page is a row, served at a content-hashed URL with an immutable year-long cache. Even the fonts are rows. Few files, full speed.

No commit-to-create

A new site is an API call, not a repository. The only committed code is the generic renderer library every tenant shares — everything else is rows.

Founding a city

Running in one command

Docker is the only requirement. On first start the app container migrates every schema and raises the default tenant — the site you are reading now — next to a remote MCP endpoint. Then hand an agent a token, let it build, review the draft in the Studio, and publish.

The full quickstart, including MCP setup
sh — from zero to served
$ git clone https://github.com/Galaktis/uruk && cd uruk
$ docker compose up -d
app   migrating public + tenant schemas, seeding the default site…
app   Listening at: http://0.0.0.0:8000
mcp   Listening at: http://0.0.0.0:8001  (/mcp)
# any hostname you point at it now serves this site

Around 3200 BC, in a Mesopotamian city called Uruk, someone pressed the first written signs into wet clay. They were not poems. They were records: heads of cattle, jars of beer, measures of grain — data, structured and stored so a city could function. The earliest human being whose name we know, Kushim, was not a king or a priest. He was an accountant signing grain ledgers.
Writing was invented as a database. Literature came two centuries later, almost as a side effect.
The web went the other way

The web began as documents and grew into codebases. Today a marketing site with four pages routinely owns a repository, a dependency tree, a build pipeline, and a deploy queue. Changing a sentence means a commit, a review, a build, and a wait. The content — the thing the site exists for — is buried inside artifacts of software engineering that have nothing to say about it.
A site is a record, not a build

Uruk stores a website the way Uruk stored grain: as rows. Pages form a URL tree; elements form composition trees; assets and settings are rows beside them. The only committed code is a small library of generic renderers shared by every site. Editing is a write. Serving is a read. Creating a whole new site is an API call that finishes before a CI pipeline would have started.

Structured records want a structured editor. Uruk's first admin client is not a dashboard but an MCP server: an AI agent authenticates as a tenant user and edits the site with exactly that user's permissions — no parallel authorization model, no special agent backdoor. The scribe changed; the ledger did not.

One Postgres holds everything: content, users, permissions, assets, settings, even this manifesto. Backup is a database dump. Portability is a JSON archive keyed by UUIDv7 — a whole site restores anywhere, ids intact. There is no state smeared across a filesystem, an object store, and a git history.

𒀕𒆠 — Uruk. The city where writing, and with it recorded data, began. The sign 𒆠 (KI) marks a place. Five thousand years on, this project makes a modest claim in the same spirit: every place on the web is, underneath everything, a record. Uruk just refuses to pretend otherwise.

Architecture

How a request becomes a page

One deployment, one Postgres, many sites. Tenant routing runs first on every request: the Host header resolves to a Domain row, the connection's search_path switches to that tenant's schema, and from that moment every query — pages, elements, users, assets — can only see one site's world.

The two right-hand stages almost never run. Computed HTML is cached per page, and a dependency graph keeps that cache honest — which is the part of a CMS that is usually wrong, and the part Uruk treats as the core of the design.

Data model

Five tables tell the story

Every row carries a UUIDv7 key and timestamps. Everything below lives in the tenant's own schema and travels with the site.

Element

A node in the composition tree: a kind that selects its renderer, JSON parameters, free content, and a parent. Reusable ones — this site's header — are included by reference wherever needed.

Page

A node in the URL tree: slug under a parent, unique per level, plus the root_element it renders from. The path /blog/my-post is just a walk down this tree.

Asset

CSS, JS, images, fonts — bytes in the database with a sha256 content hash, served immutable at /_assets/<hash>/<name>. A change is a new hash, so caches never lie.

Setting

Namespaced JSON configuration. This site's <head> — stylesheet link, favicon — is the site.head_html setting, data like everything else.

PageDependency

The reverse index behind exact invalidation: which elements each page's cached output was built from. Written on render, consulted on every save.

Tenant · Domain

The only shared tables, in the public schema: which schemas exist and which hostnames select them. Unmatched hosts fall back to the default tenant — this site.

Invalidation, the hard part

Caching rendered HTML is trivial; evicting the right entries is not, because elements are shared across pages. Uruk records the full dependency set at render time, then listens on element save and delete signals. One edit to the header element evicts the four pages that reference it and no others. Deletions survive long enough to be found because the index stores bare UUIDs, not foreign keys.

The renderer records dependencies through references: when a reusable element is included on a page, editing it invalidates every page that showed it — the exactness is structural, not heuristic.

Portability

Because every key is a UUIDv7, a whole site serializes to one JSON archive — elements, pages, assets (bytes included), settings — and restores onto any other Uruk with ids intact and zero collisions. The site you are reading is itself seeded from such an archive on first boot. 

{
  "uruk_archive_version": 1,
  "tenant":   { "name": "Uruk" },
  "elements": [ … every block of this site … ],
  "pages":    [ … /, /manifesto, /architecture, /quickstart … ],
  "assets":   [ … css, js, fonts, favicon — bytes and hashes … ],
  "settings": [ … site.head_html … ]
}

Quickstart

From zero to a served site

You need Docker (for Postgres and Redis), Python 3.15 and uv. Nothing else — no Node, no bundler, no template directory.

1 · Raise the city

On first start, migrations run for the public schema and every tenant schema; the default tenant is created, seeded with this site, and published. The website answers on port 8000, the remote MCP endpoint on 8001.

sh
$ git clone https://github.com/Galaktis/uruk && cd uruk
$ docker compose up -d
# http://localhost:8000 — any hostname serves the default tenant
# http://localhost:8001/mcp — the remote MCP endpoint

2 · Claim the throne

No credentials live in the startup path. The tenant's first superuser is claimed over the API with a claim code that only the server's operator can read (it is printed in the app's logs while the tenant is unclaimed). URUK_ADMIN_EMAIL restricts the claim to one address; once claimed, the endpoint refuses forever. Then sign in at /uruk/. Details on the configuration page.

sh
$ docker compose exec app uv run python manage.py claim_code
3f9c…  # the default tenant's claim code
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/bootstrap -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"email\": \"you@example.com\", \"code\": \"<claim code>\"}"
{"set_password_url": "/api/set-password?uid=…&token=…"}  # one-shot; a second claim is refused

3 · Hand a scribe the stylus

Issue an API token for a tenant user (the claimed superuser's username is its email), then point an MCP client at the remote endpoint. The agent can do exactly what that user's permissions allow — create pages, move elements, upload assets, publish.

sh
$ docker compose exec app uv run python manage.py create_api_token default you@example.com
uruk_…  # shown once — store it
// in an MCP client config (Claude Code, etc.)
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "uruk": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://localhost:8001/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer uruk_…" }
    }
  }
}

4 · Review, then publish

Every edit is an ordinary write to the site's draft. Visitors keep the published revision while editors watch the draft at /_preview/ — or sign in at /admin/ and open the Studio to review the agent's work, fix it, and publish. Every publish is kept: roll back to any revision, or discard the draft.

This page — the one explaining the system — is itself rows in the default tenant. Ask your agent to reword this paragraph and publish, refresh, and it's done. No commit, no build, no deploy.

Configuration

The environment is the config

Uruk reads everything from URUK_* environment variables at startup — no committed .env, no settings file to fork, no per-site configuration at all. Per-site state lives in the database like everything else; the environment only tells the process where that database is and how to behave. A process holding nothing but database credentials boots, migrates, seeds this site, and serves.

Claiming the first superuser

A fresh tenant has no users, so there is nobody to log in as. The one-shot bootstrap endpoint solves this: POST /api/bootstrap with an email creates the tenant's first superuser and returns a single-use set-password link. Because the link goes to whoever asks, the claim also needs the tenant's claim code, derived from the secret key so that only the operator can read it: manage.py bootstrap prints it in the server logs while the tenant is unclaimed, and manage.py claim_code prints it on demand. Set URUK_ADMIN_EMAIL and only that address is honoured as well. Once a superuser exists, the endpoint refuses forever — from then on, only an existing superuser can create another.

The rule is per tenant: every newly created tenant starts unclaimed, and its first superuser is caught the same way on its own domain. The walkthrough lives on the quickstart page.

Core

VariableDefaultPurpose
URUK_DEBUGFalseDjango debug mode. Keep it off anywhere real.
URUK_ENVunknownFree-form environment label — production, staging, a laptop.
URUK_SECRET_KEYinsecure dev keySigns sessions and JWTs. Set at least 32 bytes in production.
URUK_ALLOWED_HOSTS*Comma-separated Host allowlist. Uruk routes by hostname, so the catch-all default is deliberate.
URUK_BEHIND_PROXYFalseHTTPS ends at a proxy (Cloudflare Tunnel, Caddy, a load balancer): trust its X-Forwarded-Proto and mark cookies Secure. Enable only when the proxy is the sole way in.
URUK_CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINSemptyExtra scheme://host origins allowed to post forms, for proxies that rewrite the Host.

Database

VariableDefaultPurpose
URUK_DB_HOST127.0.0.1Postgres host. One database holds every tenant, each in its own schema.
URUK_DB_PORT5433Postgres port — matches the port the bundled compose file publishes.
URUK_DB_NAMEurukDatabase name.
URUK_DB_USERurukDatabase user.
URUK_DB_PASSWORDurukDatabase password.
URUK_DB_POOLTrueNative psycopg3 connection pooling — no external pooler needed.

Cache & asset storage

By default one Postgres holds everything — computed pages cache in a shared table, asset bytes live in rows. Two variables opt out when scale demands it.

VariableDefaultPurpose
URUK_REDIS_URLunsetPoint at Redis and the page/fragment cache moves there. Unset, it lives in Postgres.
URUK_STORAGE_BACKENDunsetWhere asset bytes live: unset = in the database; filesystem or boto move the bytes out (rows and hashes stay).
URUK_STORAGE_ROOT—Filesystem backend: directory for the bytes.
URUK_STORAGE_BUCKET—Boto backend: S3-compatible bucket.
URUK_STORAGE_PREFIX—Boto backend: key prefix inside the bucket.
URUK_STORAGE_ENDPOINT_URL—Boto backend: custom endpoint (MinIO, R2, …).
URUK_STORAGE_REGION—Boto backend: bucket region.

Server

Read by docker-entrypoint.sh, which forwards each to Granian — the Rust HTTP server Uruk ships on — as the matching GRANIAN_* option. The defaults are the production configuration; set a variable only to depart from them. Any other Granian option can be set directly as GRANIAN_*.

VariableDefaultPurpose
URUK_WORKERS2Worker processes. Each holds its own connection pool — keep workers × pool size under Postgres max_connections.
URUK_BLOCKING_THREADS8Request threads per worker — keep close to the connection pool's max size.
URUK_BACKPRESSURE16Maximum in-flight requests per worker.
URUK_RESPAWN_FAILED_WORKERStrueA worker that crashes comes back on its own.
URUK_WORKERS_LIFETIME3600Recycle each worker after this many seconds.
URUK_WORKERS_MAX_RSS512Recycle a worker as soon as its memory exceeds this many MiB.

Bootstrap

VariableDefaultPurpose
URUK_DEFAULT_TENANT_SCHEMAdefaultSchema name of the catch-all tenant — the one serving this page to any unmatched hostname.
URUK_DEFAULT_TENANT_DOMAINdefault.localhostPlaceholder primary domain recorded for it. Routing to the default tenant is by fallback, not by matching this string.
URUK_DEFAULT_SITEshowcaseWhat the default tenant starts with: showcase (this website) or blank (one empty landing page to fill in).
URUK_ADMIN_EMAILemptyRestrict the first-superuser claim to this address, on top of the claim code. Empty = any address.
URUK_ADMIN_PATHurukURL prefix of the Django admin and its login page. Off the well-known /admin/; it shadows a page with the same top-level slug.

JWT

VariableDefaultPurpose
URUK_JWT_ACCESS_TTL900Access-token lifetime, seconds (15 minutes).
URUK_JWT_REFRESH_TTL1209600Refresh-token lifetime, seconds (14 days).

Observability

The one family that keeps its standard names: the OpenTelemetry SDK reads OTEL_* variables itself, so Uruk does not rename them. The rule stays the same — nothing loads unless configured. Without an endpoint the SDK is never even imported; with one, requests, database and cache activity are traced, and every request span carries the resolved tenant schema as uruk.tenant.

VariableDefaultPurpose
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINTunsetThe gate. Point at an OTLP/HTTP collector and tracing turns on; unset, telemetry costs nothing.
OTEL_SERVICE_NAMEurukService name on exported spans.
any other OTEL_*—Headers, sampling, resource attributes — every standard OpenTelemetry SDK variable applies as-is.

MCP

Read by the MCP server process — the agent's stdio bridge — not by Django itself.

VariableDefaultPurpose
URUK_MCP_TENANT—Tenant schema the agent works in.
URUK_MCP_TOKEN—The uruk_… API token it authenticates with; the agent gets exactly that user's permissions.
